title: Fathers used Church consensus against heretics — not present-pastor supremacy
source_text: XXXIX. Ad illam vero argumenti confirmationem, quae inde petita est quod Ecclesiae Doctores, ad confutandos varios haereticos, qui quosdam Scripturae libros repudiabant, perpetuo usi sunt testimonio & consensu Ecclesiae, quo librorum istorum authoritatem comprobarunt: Respondeo, inde minime concludi posse quod Pontificii volunt, & quod in quaestione est, nempe authoritatem Pastorum, qui unoquoque saeculo Ecclesiam gubernant, majorem quoad nos & notiorem esse Scripturae authoritate, fidemque nostram de Scriptura niti testimonio & judicio Pastorum qui jam Ecclesiae praesunt tanquam divino & infallibili, & tanquam praecipuo & proprio suo fundamento. Neque Doctores isti simpliciter argumentantur ex Episcoporum sui temporis authoritate, quasi regula fidei fuisset, & ea singulorum Ecclesiae membrorum fides obstringeretur: sed, quum haeretici illi, quos impugnabant, librorum quorundam sacrorum authoritatem rejicerent, quasi Apostolis aut viris Apostolicis falso tribuerentur, & a Catholicis Doctoribus conficti essent, Patres illis opposuerunt perpetuum Episcoporum atque fidelium consensum, qui jam inde ab Apostolorum temporibus, libros illos venerati sunt tanquam ab Apostolis traditos & commendatos pro veris & divinis: cui consensui fidem derogare non potest, nisi homo protervus & pervicax. Etenim, si ille qui hodie negaret libros Aristotelis, Demosthenis & Ciceronis, eorum esse quibus tribuuntur, convinci posset ex consensu Doctorum, qui omnibus saeculis libros illos tribuerunt magnis illis & praestantibus viris, & insanus haberetur qui famae tam constanti & celebri fidem denegaret: Annon pari, imo longe majori jure insanus habeatur, qui se audet opponere traditioni, & famae constantiori & celebriori, & magis adhuc continuae, quae libros illos, quos pro sacris habemus, ad Apostolos refert tanquam authores & approbatores?
pass_a_gloss: But to that confirmation of the argument which is drawn from this, that the Doctors of the Church, for confuting various heretics who repudiated certain books of Scripture, continually used the testimony and consensus of the Church by which they proved the authority of those books: I answer that from this it can least of all be concluded what the Pontificians want, and what is in question — namely that the authority of the Pastors who in each age govern the Church is greater as regards us and better known than the authority of Scripture, and that our faith concerning Scripture rests on the testimony and judgment of the Pastors who now preside over the Church as on something divine and infallible, and as on its chief and proper foundation. Nor do those Doctors simply argue from the authority of the Bishops of their own time, as if it had been a rule of faith, and by it the faith of the individual members of the Church were bound: but, when those heretics whom they were attacking rejected the authority of certain sacred books, as if they were falsely ascribed to the Apostles or Apostolic men and had been fabricated by Catholic Doctors, the Fathers opposed to them the perpetual consensus of Bishops and of the faithful who, already from the times of the Apostles, have venerated those books as handed down and recommended by the Apostles for true and divine: and from that consensus faith cannot be withdrawn except by a man who is shameless and stubborn. For if he who today would deny that the books of Aristotle, Demosthenes, and Cicero are of those to whom they are ascribed could be convinced from the consensus of the learned who in all ages have ascribed those books to those great and excellent men, and would be held insane who denied credit to a fame so constant and celebrated: Should he not by equal — indeed by far greater — right be held insane who dares to oppose a tradition and a fame more constant and more celebrated, and still more continuous, which refers those books which we hold as sacred to the Apostles as authors and approvers?
pass_b_english: As for that supporting point — that the Church's doctors, when they answered heretics who rejected certain books of Scripture, kept using the Church's testimony and consensus to prove those books' authority — I answer that this does not yield what the Pontificians want, or what is actually in dispute.

It does not show that the pastors who govern the Church in each age have, for us, an authority greater and better known than Scripture's, or that our faith about Scripture rests on the testimony and judgment of the pastors now in office as on a divine, infallible, chief, and proper foundation.
Those fathers were not simply arguing from the authority of the bishops of their own day as if that were a rule of faith binding every church member.

The heretics they opposed rejected certain sacred books as falsely ascribed to the apostles or apostolic men and as inventions of Catholic teachers. Against that charge the Fathers set the perpetual consensus of bishops and of the faithful who, from the apostles' time on, have received those books as handed down and recommended by the apostles as true and divine.

Only a shameless, stubborn person can refuse that consensus. Anyone today who denied that the books of Aristotle, Demosthenes, and Cicero belong to the men named on them could be answered from the continuous judgment of the learned who have always ascribed them so — and would be thought mad for refusing so constant a fame.

By equal — indeed by far greater — right, then, is the person mad who dares to oppose a tradition and fame still more constant, celebrated, and continuous, which refers the books we hold sacred to the apostles as their authors and approvers?

lemmas.gloss: testimony and consensus of the Church

choices.why: Moral refusal of known consensus, not mere error.
